description:
We’re a team of three engineers who believe 3:15 is the perfect time: the clock hands are almost aligned, like the Sun, Earth and Moon before a good landing.

We’re building a CLPS Lunar Mission Browser that makes choosing where and when to land on the Moon as easy as booking a weekend getaway.

We bring computer vision, 3D and multi-view geometry, deep math, coding and system design expertise, data science from spreadsheets to multimodal LLMs, and peak productivity at 3:15 AM.
summary:
Lunar Site Explorer is a web app that answers one question for south-pole missions: is this landing site and date viable, and what changes if the date slips? We built it on real NASA LOLA terrain and JPL/NAIF ephemerides. For any site (catalogue or custom coordinates) and date, it shows the Sun and Earth against the ray-traced terrain horizon, time to sunset and Earthset, illumination, Earth visibility and direct-to-Earth windows.
Planners can compare scenarios side by side and drag a "what if the launch slips by N days" slider. A map mode with live shadows and a transparent suitability score finds the best spots, and a first-person panorama lets anyone stand on the site and see the Sun and Earth at true angular size. It also estimates how tall an antenna must be to see the Earth. The tool turns scattered ephemeris and topography data into clear, comparable visuals for mission planners, educators and the public. It runs in the browser from open NASA data.
details:
What it does. Lunar Site Explorer helps mission planners, educators and the public judge a lunar south-pole landing site in seconds. At the pole the Sun never rises above ~1.5°, so mountains tens of kilometres away decide when a lander has power and a line of sight to Earth. We compute that from real data and show it in three linked views:

• Map: south-polar stereographic map with a custom WebGL2 engine. Terrain is lit live by the real Sun with ray-traced shadows and the finite solar disk. Layers: illumination, Earth visibility, slope, and a transparent suitability score (slope limit, sunlight, longest night, Earth contact) with a "Find best spots" search inside the 80°S coverage and ranking robustness.

• Sky plot and metrics: terrain horizon silhouette (±1σ from LOLA error maps), Sun and Earth tracks with libration, close-ups of the discs clipped by ridges, countdown to sunset/Earthset, direct-to-Earth windows.

• Panorama: first-person view on 5 m LOLA terrain with ray-marched soft shadows, Sun and Earth at true angular size (Earth with phase), WASD walking and time-lapse.

Suitability finds known sites on its own. The suitability score knows nothing about site catalogues: it only sees terrain, sunlight, night length and Earth contact. Yet when "Find best spots" picks candidates automatically, they often land at, or right next to, the south-pole sites that NASA already studied with LOLA 5 m digital elevation maps (for example near Leibnitz beta plateau and Nobile rim 1). Our unsupervised ranking rediscovers the places that mission planners independently consider the best, which is a strong sign that the score captures the right physics.


Scenario comparison. Up to four site/date scenarios side by side, timelines, a heat calendar and a "what if it slips by N days" slider. Example from our own scan: a 10-day slip on the connecting ridge drops 14-day sunlight from 89% to 24% and raises the longest night from 5 h to 108 h.

Antenna analysis. For any antenna height (1 m to 100 m) the app recomputes the Earth horizon and shows how tall the antenna must be to reach the Earth, as a distribution over time. If more than 1 km is needed, it reports "no link".

Accuracy. No atmosphere, so the horizon is terrain plus the lunar limb. We use the Moon's real topography, libration (MOON_ME frame, DE440), and horizon ray-marching 300 km out. Results were validated against JPL Horizons and published illumination maps.

Impact. The tool closes the gap between detailed analysis tools (Quickmap, Moon Trek, Horizons) and fast, comparable answers. It helps teams react when schedules slip, and it explains to students and the public why the Moon is hard.

Tools. TypeScript, Preact, @preact/signals, OpenLayers, custom WebGL2 engine, Vite. Python with NumPy, Numba, rasterio/GDAL, SpiceyPy (NAIF SPICE), optional FastAPI compute service for region-scale heatmaps and Monte-Carlo robustness. Docker Compose, nginx, Caddy (automatic HTTPS), DigitalOcean droplet. Core features run fully client-side, so static hosting also works.

Creativity. One interface for experts and non-experts, a real-terrain sky plot instead of raw ephemeris tables, a panorama that shows the same numbers as a place you can stand in, and a data-driven antenna-height answer.

Factors considered. Data accuracy and its uncertainty (LOLA error maps), reproducibility (one make bootstrap builds everything from public NASA data), and performance on ordinary laptops.

Mazarico et al. Sun/Earth visibility maps (validation)
LRO LOLA gridded global DEM LDEM_16 (PDS Geosciences Node)
NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE generic kernels (de440s, lunar PCK and frame kernels)
NASA SVS south-pole illumination visualizations (sanity check)
NASA CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services), context for sites
